title: After the Bombs at Metal Sider, Issad Rebrab Bought One Cargo of Sugar
dek: In January 1995 an armed group destroyed Issad Rebrab's steel works during Algeria's civil war; he began again small, one shipload at a time.

story.event: Starting again after his steel works was bombed during Algeria's civil war
story.summary: In January 1995, during Algeria's civil war, an armed group destroyed the Metal Sider steel works of the Algerian industrialist Issad Rebrab, who said he had also received death threats and left for France for a time. He started again in small steps, with butcher shops in France and trial cargoes of imported sugar, and in 1998 founded Cevital, building an edible-oil refinery on the port of Béjaïa.
paragraphs: In January 1995, at the height of Algeria's civil war, an armed group destroyed the Metal Sider steel works near Algiers. The BBC later reported that 14 bombs reduced the plant to rubble; other accounts speak of some fifty gunmen, and of attacks on three of the owner's largest sites. The owner was Issad Rebrab, a former accountancy teacher from a Kabyle village who had set up as a chartered accountant in 1968 and moved into metalwork in 1971. Metal Sider, founded in 1988, had begun producing in 1992 and quickly became the core of his fortune. He later put the damage at about 1.1 billion dinars.

Rebrab said he had also received death threats. He left Algeria for France. Accounts differ on how long he stayed, from a few months to about two years. He did not stop working. In France, the BBC reported, he started again with butcher shops in Paris that made modest profits, part of a halal meat business he had begun earlier.

The way back was cautious. Working with two of his sons, he turned to importing sugar into Algeria, where foreign trade had recently been opened to private firms. By the BBC's account he bought one shipload as a first test, then a second, then a third, until the trade paid well. From 1997 a Hyundai car dealership added cash. Cevital, the company he founded in 1998, still gives his motto as « Voir grand, commencer petit et aller vite »: think big, start small, move fast.

Cevital's first large venture was an edible-oil refinery on the port of Béjaïa, competing with state monopolies in oil and then sugar. When Jeune Afrique visited in 2013, the site covered 14 hectares, part of it reclaimed from the sea, and the magazine reported that since 1998 he had made each new unit earn the money to finance the next and repay its loans. Cevital by then exported sugar to some twenty countries and was Algeria's largest private company.

quote.text: men should furnish themselves with such things as would float, and might with the owner escape the storm
quote.translator: Charles Cotton (1685), ed. W. C. Hazlitt
quote.source_title: Essays of Michel de Montaigne — Complete, tr. Charles Cotton, Project Gutenberg eBook #3600
quote.connection: Montaigne passes on Antisthenes' advice to own what can float. Rebrab's steel works could not leave with him. His trade, his feel for numbers and his habit of testing one shipload before risking the next could, and they were what he rebuilt from.

reflection: Most of what Rebrab had built was fixed to the ground, and an attack took it. What he carried out was less visible: an accountant's way of reading numbers, trades he understood, and a willingness to begin again with one cargo instead of a whole industry.

You will not, I hope, face anything like that. But it is worth knowing which parts of your work would float: the judgement you have built, the people who trust you, the habits that steady you on bad days. Those deserve looking after too, and they tend to grow in rest more than in rush.
invitation: Write one sentence naming a skill or a relationship of yours that no failed project could take away. Put it somewhere you will see it on a harder day.

cross_checks.claim: In 1995, during the civil war, Rebrab's main Metal Sider steel installations were destroyed in an attack by an armed group
Feeling threatened, he left Algeria for France for a time
He put the damage at about 1.1 billion dinars (his own figure)
He restarted with sugar imports into Algeria
He founded Cevital in 1998 with an edible-oil refinery at the port of Béjaïa

research_notes: No first-person account of the attack could be read: Rebrab's own words survive mainly through French Wikipedia's quotation of a TSA biography that is now offline (404), Le Monde's profiles could not be loaded without a browser, and his own site (issadrebrab.org) did not respond. The story therefore rests on independent reports and attributes his own claims (death threats, the cost). The attack: BBC Arabic (2019) says 14 bombs destroyed the Metal Sider plant in January 1995; Noonpost (2022) says about 50 armed men stormed and blew up the main plant that month; Observ'Algérie, Afrik.com and Family Business Histories speak of three of his largest sites. The story gives these as differing accounts. Cost: Family Business Histories gives 1.1 billion dinars (French Wikipedia quotes Rebrab giving the same figure to TSA); Observ'Algérie converts his figure to more than 6 million euros in today's money and Family Business Histories to about $15.5 million in 2022 terms. The story gives only his dinar figure. Length of exile: 'a few months' (Afrik.com, Leaders League) against a return in 1997 (Family Business Histories); the story says accounts differ. The halal meat business (Isla Mondial) was founded in 1992 according to Observ'Algérie, before the exile, while BBC Arabic describes butcher shops he opened in Paris after leaving; the story says he started again with shops that were part of a business begun earlier. The 1995 liberalisation of foreign trade comes from Noonpost; the story says only that trade had recently been opened to private firms. Noonpost and others argue that political connections helped his rise; that is not adjudicated here. His 2019 detention, the main subject of the BBC Arabic article, is a separate episode and is not told. The Jeune Afrique profile carries an archive date of 4 November 2008 but describes events of 2007. The motto is quoted in French as Cevital publishes it, with an English gloss. The Antisthenes line is reported by Montaigne in 'Of Solitude', where it concerns inner possessions; it is applied here by analogy to skills that survive the loss of property.
